tasks.short: Find the manual and drawings for the machine, read and understand them for the job, ask the foreman about unclear drawings, and take printed pages to the machine.

steps.what: Heavy equipment mechanic finds the right manual and drawings for the machine model and serial number
Heavy equipment mechanic reads and understands operating manuals, blueprints and hydraulic drawings for the job
Heavy equipment mechanic asks the workshop foreman about unclear drawings
Heavy equipment mechanic prints pages and takes them to the machine

tasks.design: The work order in the workshop system ({OPS_SYSTEM}) carries the machine's model and serial number and opens the matching manual and drawings in the manufacturer's service portal ({PARTNER_PORTAL}) on a rugged tablet that goes to the machine. Reading the drawings and asking the foreman stay with the mechanic.
tasks.previous_blocker: Manuals were searched by model in binders and portals, and pages printed for the yard.
tasks.enabler_now: Manufacturer service portals open documents by serial number, and rugged tablets work in the yard.
tasks.still_hard: Older or modified machines do not match the drawings.
tasks.human_edge: Seeing that a previous owner rerouted a hydraulic line the drawing still shows.

evidence.claim: Manufacturer service portals open manuals and drawings by machine serial number for licensed workshops.

assumptions: Boundary: from the work order to pages at the machine; the repair is outside.
Input contract: work orders with serial numbers from the service planner; documents from the manufacturer's portal under the workshop's licence; fallback is binders and printing.
Reading and asking do not change.
The workshop holds portal licences for the brands it repairs.
research_questions: Does document search time fall per job?

incremental.description: Heavy equipment mechanic charges and looks after the tablet.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: a mixed fleet of older brands without portal access, so most documents are still found in binders and printed (5.2); high: a few brands with portal licences (21.5).

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Connect the tester and read fault codes, test pressures and sensors to diagnose the fault, look up code meanings and test steps, and write the diagnosis on the work order.

steps.what: Heavy equipment mechanic connects the diagnostic tester and reads fault codes
Heavy equipment mechanic looks up what each fault code means and its test steps
Heavy equipment mechanic diagnoses faults by testing hydraulic pressures, sensors and calibration
Heavy equipment mechanic writes the diagnosis and required repairs on the work order

tasks.design: Machines with telematics send their fault codes and hour readings to the work order ({OPS_SYSTEM}) before the mechanic arrives, so the tester is needed less often just to read codes. Each code links to its meaning and test steps in the manufacturer's service information. The diagnosis goes on the work order in fixed fields with the codes filled in. Testing and diagnosing stay with the mechanic.
tasks.previous_blocker: Codes were read on site with a tester and looked up in separate service manuals.
tasks.enabler_now: Machine telematics push fault codes, and service information links codes to test steps.
tasks.still_hard: Many hydraulic faults leave no code at all.
tasks.human_edge: Hearing a pump cavitate before any sensor reports it.

reach.learn: Whether codes before the visit get the right parts on the first trip.

evidence.claim: Telematics on newer heavy equipment report fault codes and hour readings remotely.
If work order time stamps are used to watch technician speed, the works council must consent first.

assumptions: Boundary: from the fault report to the repair plan; the repair itself is outside.
Input contract: fault reports from operators or telematics; service information from the manufacturer; fallback is the tester and manuals.

Testing and diagnosing keep their full time. s1 keeps 70 because only telematics machines send codes ahead; s3 keeps 50 for reading the linked test steps; s4 keeps 90 because the codes fill in and the mechanic still writes the diagnosis and repairs.
Older machines without telematics keep the tester.

incremental.description: Heavy equipment mechanic checks telematics codes against what the machine shows.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: an older fleet with few telematics units, so the tester is still connected for most codes (9.0); high: a newer fleet that reports codes remotely (14.0).

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Research part numbers, check stock, compare suppliers, decide and place the parts order, restock the parts store and record parts used on the work order.

steps.what: Heavy equipment mechanic researches part numbers in parts books and the manufacturer portal
Heavy equipment mechanic checks the parts store for stock
Heavy equipment mechanic phones dealers for price and delivery
Heavy equipment mechanic decides what to order and from whom
Heavy equipment mechanic checks the final order: parts, quantities, dealer, price and delivery address
Heavy equipment mechanic orders the parts from the dealer: by phone today, from the work order through the dealer portal after the change
Heavy equipment mechanic counts and restocks the parts inventory
Heavy equipment mechanic writes parts used on the work order

tasks.design: The work order opens the parts list for the machine's serial number in the manufacturer portal ({PARTNER_PORTAL}) and shows stock from the workshop system ({OPS_SYSTEM}). Dealer prices and delivery times come from the dealers' ordering portals where they exist. Once the mechanic has decided and checked the final order, the mechanic sends it once to the dealer from the work order. Parts are scanned at receipt and at issue, so stock stays current, only a short shelf check remains, and parts used land on the work order.
tasks.previous_blocker: Parts were looked up in books, stock checked by walking to the store and orders phoned in.
tasks.enabler_now: Dealer portals take orders and workshop systems track stock by scan.
tasks.still_hard: Parts for older machines often need a phone call and a pattern supplier.
tasks.human_edge: Knowing a cheaper pattern part that fits and lasts.
tasks.altitude: The mechanic decides orders instead of chasing numbers and prices.

evidence.claim: OutSmart covers the work order from job to invoice.
If work order time stamps are used to watch technician speed, the works council must consent first.

assumptions: Boundary: from the repair plan to parts on the work order; paying invoices is outside.
Input contract: repair plans from the mechanic's diagnosis; parts lists from the manufacturer portal; dealer prices from dealer portals; fallback is books and phone.

Deciding and the order check stay with the mechanic and keep their full time; orders above the spending limit follow the workshop's existing approval. s5 keeps 20 for sending the order; s6 keeps 60 because restocking stays and only full counts go; s7 keeps 30 for checking parts that landed from issue scans.
Dealers' time is outside the mechanic's savings.
research_questions: Do repairs wait less for parts?

incremental.description: Heavy equipment mechanic labels bins and fixes scan errors.

approvals.approved_version: The order with parts, quantities, price and delivery address exactly as checked by the mechanic in s4c, sent once to the chosen dealer's ordering portal; any change needs a new check.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: many older machines whose parts and prices still need books and phone calls (35.2); high: brands with dealer portals (45.7).

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Read hour meters and service intervals, schedule maintenance with the planner, keep equipment service records, check records are complete and report machines back in service.

steps.what: Heavy equipment mechanic reads hour meters and service intervals per machine
Heavy equipment mechanic schedules maintenance with the fleet planner
Heavy equipment mechanic writes the service done: in the paper equipment service records today, on a tablet checklist per machine after the change
Heavy equipment mechanic files service sheets and checks records are complete
Heavy equipment mechanic checks the machine is ready for release: service done, record complete and no open defects
Heavy equipment mechanic releases the machine back to service: by phone to the planner today, in the maintenance system after the change

tasks.design: Hour readings come from telematics or a monthly reading into the maintenance system ({OPS_SYSTEM}), which lists machines due for service. The fleet planner sees the same due list, so the mechanic agrees service slots in fewer calls. The mechanic records service on a tablet checklist per machine in about the time the logbook took, a missing-records view replaces filing checks, and once the mechanic has checked the machine and its record the mechanic releases it to the planner in the system.
tasks.previous_blocker: Intervals were tracked in a spreadsheet and service written in paper logbooks.
tasks.enabler_now: Maintenance systems take hour readings and hold service checklists per machine.
tasks.still_hard: Machines on remote sites miss their readings and slots.
tasks.human_edge: Moving a service forward because a machine sounds tired before its hours say so.

reach.learn: Whether release messages cut idle days.

evidence.claim: In a two-month parallel run, a paper technical log had 52 errors and an electronic log had 1 (aviation vendor case).
If log time stamps are used to watch technician speed, the works council must consent first.

assumptions: Boundary: from the fleet list to the machine released; the service work itself is outside.
Input contract: fleet list and intervals kept by the fleet planner; hour readings from telematics or operators; fallback is the spreadsheet and logbook.

Agreeing slots stays a conversation; s2 keeps 80 because the shared due list saves some calls. Writing the service done is a first record and keeps its full time; the release check keeps its full time; s4 keeps 50 and s5 keeps 20.
The fleet planner's time is outside the mechanic's savings.

already_counted.description: Heavy equipment mechanic reviews the due list.

incremental.description: Heavy equipment mechanic enters readings for machines without telematics.

approvals.approved_version: The machine's return to service with its service record exactly as checked by the mechanic in s4c, released once to the fleet planner in the maintenance system; any change needs a new check.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: an older fleet with manual hour readings, so most due dates are still worked out by hand (23.2); high: telematics on most machines (29.2).

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

role.altitude: The heavy equipment mechanic keeps diagnosing, reading drawings and deciding parts; searching documents, phone orders and paper logbooks shrink.
skills_to_grow: Working from tablets and telematics data
role.ambitious_version: A mechanic who arrives at the machine with codes, parts and drawings ready.

job.title: Mobile Heavy Equipment Mechanics, Except Engines
